description: Los Galacticos is a three-person student team from Istanbul combining cybersecurity and computer engineering to build privacy-first health monitoring software for astronauts.
summary:
Mars Transit Crew Monitor is a web dashboard that helps a crew and ground control track astronaut health and cabin air during a Mars transit, where a one-way radio delay of 3-22 minutes means the crew must act before Earth can reply.

A simulator streams live crew vitals (heart rate, SpO2, respiration, temperature, HRV) and cabin conditions (O2 partial pressure, CO2, pressure, humidity, radiation). A rules engine compares every reading with each person's own baseline and with reference ranges from NASA-STD-3001 where available, then raises Normal, Watch, Warning or Action alerts with plain-language recommendations. Six replayable scenarios demonstrate it: nominal operation, hypoxia, CO2 rise, a solar storm (using the time and type of a real NASA DONKI event) and sensor dropout. Missing data is never shown as normal; it is flagged as unknown. Reports to Earth wait in a queue with realistic light delay, and replies are simulated.

It matters because on a Mars mission, early and clear warnings can help the crew act when help is minutes away. All crew data and radiation doses are simulated, and personal-deviation thresholds are unverified team assumptions, so this is a demonstration, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mars Transit Crew Monitor streams simulated crew vitals (heart rate, SpO2, respiration rate, core temperature, HRV) and cabin conditions (O2 partial pressure, CO2, pressure, temperature, humidity, radiation dose rate) to a live Mission Control style dashboard. A rules engine compares each reading with the person's own baseline and with reference ranges, and raises Normal, Watch, Warning or Action alerts with plain-language recommendations. Six replayable scenarios show it working: nominal operation, hypoxia (O2 unit failure while a crew member exercises), CO2 rise, a solar storm and sensor dropout.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On a Mars transit, one-way radio delay is 3-22 minutes, so the crew cannot wait for Earth to interpret a problem. The tool gives early, consistent, easy-to-read warnings on board, and queues reports to Earth with realistic light delay so the team can see what ground control knows and when.

NASA DATA AND RESOURCES

- Cabin limits (O2 partial pressure, CO2, pressure, suit CO2) come from NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 and NASA OCHMO-TB-004.

- Radiation: the 600 mSv career limit and the 250 mSv design threshold for a reference solar particle event (a vehicle shielding requirement, used here as an alert threshold) come from NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1.

- The solar storm scenario uses the time and type of a real NASA DONKI solar particle event (2024-05-10). DONKI does not give dose, so all dose values are simulated and labeled.

HOW IT IS BUILT

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, server-sent events for the live stream, Pydantic data contract (v0.2.0).

- A simulator with a cabin mass balance for O2 and CO2, and a rules engine with consecutive-reading checks to avoid false alarms.

- Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no external CDNs or frameworks. IBM Plex fonts (SIL OFL 1.1) bundled locally.

- Quality: automated tests (500+), linting and CI on every pull request, including a test that checks WCAG AA contrast for 90 color pairs in dark and light themes.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- Missing or lost sensor data is never treated as normal: it appears as "Unknown" and raises a Watch alert.

- Alerts compare each astronaut with their own baseline, not only a population limit.

- The interface uses colorblind-safe colors (Okabe-Ito palette), status icons and text in addition to color, and respects reduced-motion settings.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delay, crew safety, false alarms versus missed alarms, accessibility, and honesty about uncertainty.

PERSONAL BASELINE THRESHOLDS

The app also flags changes in each astronaut's vitals compared with that person's own baseline. These eight thresholds are team assumptions chosen for the demo, not NASA limits, and are labeled "Unverified" in the app:

- SpO2 drop: watch at 3 percentage points, action at 6

- Resting heart rate rise: watch at 15 bpm, action at 30 bpm

- Respiratory rate rise: watch at 4 breaths/min, action at 8

- Body temperature rise: watch at 0.5 °C, action at 1 °C

Most alerts need 3 consecutive readings. The direction follows published practice: a 3-4% SpO2 drop from baseline is used in exercise oximetry, about 1 °C over baseline is used in a fever definition for older adults, and baseline-relative changes are studied for early illness detection. For heart rate and respiratory rate we found no published cutoff, so those values are our own and need clinical review. Two sleep thresholds (watch below 6 hours, action below 5 hours per sleep period) are also team assumptions and unverified. The full list and its status are in data/reference/ranges.json in our repository.

AI USE

We used Claude Code (Anthropic) to generate backend and frontend code from our specification, to draft alert texts, translations and documentation, to help check source links, and to write the motion graphics code (HyperFrames) for the 30-second demo video, which carries a visible SI watermark. We also used ChatGPT (OpenAI), DeepSeek, Mistral and GLM (Zhipu AI) for parts of the coding work, and Google Gemini (Antigravity IDE) for code review and test checks. Team members reviewed and tested every change through pull requests. AI did not choose the project idea or the thresholds, and did not generate the space weather data, which is real NASA DONKI data. Our declaration is in docs/AI_USE_DECLARATION.md in our repository.

LIMITS

All crew data and radiation doses are simulated. This is a demonstration, not a medical device, and it is not endorsed by NASA.
